title: Enhancing MMDiT-Based Text-to-Image Models for Similar Subject Generation
role: Splits similar-subject failure on SD3 into early-block attention, CLIP-versus-T5 disagreement and attention gathering in one place, and shows a step-5 overlap check that predicts failure; MMDiT-only losses, box-free.
enters: a combination: cross-attention in early blocks 5-8, the text encoder (CLIP and T5 disagree on a word's location), and layout (similar subjects' attention gathers at the same location)
enters_evidence: Qualitative: one prompt and seed per cause, attention maps at step 5 of 28 (Fig. 3); the ablation measures the fixes (three-subject Grounding DINO success 37.9% to 46.2% with block alignment, +8.6 with overlap loss, 57.3% with text-encoder loss)
changes: Gradient steps on the latent (alpha 30) against block-alignment, text-encoder-alignment and overlap losses on blocks 5-12 cross-attention, steps 1-14 of 28 with 15 iterations at steps 3-5; at step 5 a restart from the same noise blocks the worst subject from the overlap region
training: Nothing trained; needs the subject words located in the CLIP and T5 token sequences; no boxes, masks or LLM (it names Bounded Attention as needing layout masks)
model: SD3 Medium (2B), 28 steps, guidance 7.0; SD3.5 Medium in the appendix; MMDiT-specific, no UNet tested
similar_subjects: Whole benchmark is similar subjects (90 prompts x 100 seeds). Success rate (all subjects present, %, higher better) by Grounding DINO on SD3: 68.8 vs 61.9 CONFORM vs 53.1 SD3 (two); 66.7 vs 57.1 vs 37.9 (three); 52.7 vs 42.4 vs 33.1 (four)
which_pairs: Not measured per pair; argued from one example each: duck and goose gather attention in one place through shape and appearance, cat and dog split CLIP from T5, bear and panda stay mixed in blocks 5-8; dissimilar frog and bench separate from block 5
when: Step-5 (of 28) attention maps predict the final failure; overlap check at step 5 fires on 0.4%, 29.3%, 42.1% of two, three, four-subject images after the losses; widening the window to step 6 adds under 1 point
cost: 68.7 s per image vs 20.4 s plain SD3 on one A6000; 118.6 s when the restart fires; about 56 extra forward-and-backward iterations per image (inferred from Algorithm 1)
headline: Three similar subjects on SD3 Medium: Grounding DINO success rate 66.7% (67.8% with seed rejection) vs 57.1% CONFORM and 37.9% plain SD3; GPT-4o-mini 80.2% vs 72.1% vs 31.2%
suggests: (inferred) Use its overlap ratio (fraction of one subject's thresholded region covered by the other, threshold 0.2) as the cross-attention overlap predictor, record per-encoder text disagreement for SDXL's two CLIP encoders, and treat a step-early overlap check plus restart as a box-free source of regions for Bounded Attention.

disagreements.claim: SD3 success rate on similar subjects falls below 20%
disagreements.paper_says: p. 1 says the success rate drops to 'even less than 20%', but the lowest plain-SD3 rate in Table 1 (p. 8) is 22.5% (GPT-4o-mini, four subjects); it may refer to single prompts, which are not reported

disagreements.claim: Contribution list names three novel losses
disagreements.paper_says: p. 2 lists 'three novel losses represented by block alignment loss, overlap online detection and back-to-start sampling strategy', one loss and two strategies; the three losses are block alignment, text-encoder alignment and overlap (pp. 4-5)

pp. 7-8 say rejection improves success 'without any additional overhead', but rejection only happens after a restart that raises time to 118.6 s (p. 13), and the paper does not say how rejected seeds enter the success rate

quotes.text: the effect of inaccurate attention activation in earlier layers has already been incurred, which leads to semantic leakage
the activated cross-attention of subject text representations (i.e., cat and dog) from the CLIP text encoder and T5 text encoder are sometimes inconsistent
the similarity in shape and appearance of “duck” and “goose” causes their attentions are aggregated at same locations, despite the agreement between the text encoders
Generally, the first four blocks struggle to significantly differentiate between different subject semantics.
SD3 significantly distinguishes different subjects from the fifth block onwards, thus producing satisfactory results. However, for similar subjects, the 5th through 8th blocks become strained.
All cross-attention maps are from the 5th step of denoising (28 steps in total).
alignment loss Lba and overlap loss Lol bring additional success rate improvements of 8.3% and 8.6%, respectively.
alignment loss Lta boosts the success rate to 57.3%
where λba , λta , λol are set to 1, 0.2, 0.001 respectively depending on their magnitude and importance.
The latent update scale αt is set to 30. Consistent with previous methods [4, 21], latent is optimized only in the first half of the
we choose to perform multiple iterations of optimization in the early stages of denoising (steps 3-5) to trade-off between the two.
When the denoising process proceeds to step 5, we evaluate the repair effect brought by applying
a training-free manner based only on the input text without using external signals (e.g., layout masks [7]).
We deploy our approach on Stable Diffusion 3 Medium (2B).
We generated 30 prompts (e.g., “a [subjectA] and a [subjectB]”) each for descriptions with two similar subjects
For each of these 90 prompts, we generate 100 images using 100 random seeds applied across all methods.
SR (G DINO) and SR (GPT 4o) represent the Success Rate (whether or not the subjects all appear in the results)
